To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
elective cesarean delivery does not significantly decrease the risk of MTCT in HIV infected pregnant women who are on ARV prophylactic treatment.

the risk of vertical transmission of HIV in a setting where antiretrovital prophylaxis and replacement feeding is provided is less than 1% and is not statistically significantly different from the risk of vertical HIV transmission in a setting where cesarean section is provided.

the risk of vertical transmission of HIV in women with CD4 counts greater than 350 cells/μl and viral loads less than 1000 copies/ml at 36 weeks of gestation is less than 1% in a setting where replacement feeding is available and that elective cesarean delivery does not decrease the transmission risk in such cases(4).

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
elective cesarean delivery reduces the risk of vertical HIV transmission by 50% in a setting where antiretrovival therapy is not available.
elective cesarean delivery is the safest mode of delivery for HIV-infected women.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
elective cesarean delivery is not necessary if ARV prophylactic regimen is given to mother and child and if the mother is on ART.
vaginal delivery is a safe and viable alternative to cesarean section for HIV infected women in the presence of ARV prophylactic treatment and replacement feeding.
elective cesarean delivery should not be recommended in the absence of ARV prophylactic therapy for the mother and the baby.
The main takeaway from our work is that
elective cesarean delivery is not a necessary component of a comprehensive prevention of vertical transmission of HIV program.
vaginal delivery in HIV infected pregnant women is safe and viable option in the setting where ARV and replacement feeding is practiced and cesarean section is not available.
elective cesarean delivery does not have a significant impact on MTCT rates when compared to vaginal delivery in HIV-infected mothers on ARV prophylaxsis.
